pharm: Bactericidal beta-lactam that inhibits bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan synthesis; the benzathine salt provides slow release from intramuscular sites for prolonged low serum levels.
tags: Boxed warning: NOT for intravenous use
quick: Strep pharyngitis: 1,200,000 units IM x1; syphilis (early): 2,400,000 units IM x1
No evidence of fetal harm; use during pregnancy only if clearly needed
Penicillin G is excreted in breast milk; use with caution
Substantially renally excreted; toxicity risk higher in renal impairment
Hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis, injection site, follow-up cultures in strep
summary: Penicillin G benzathine (Bicillin L-A) is a long-acting intramuscular penicillin that provides low, prolonged serum levels. It is indicated for mild-to-moderate upper-respiratory streptococcal infections, venereal infections (syphilis, yaws, bejel, pinta), and prophylaxis of rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis. It carries a boxed warning that it is NOT for intravenous use: inadvertent intravenous administration has caused cardiorespiratory arrest and death. Deep intramuscular injection only, avoiding arteries and nerves.
indications: Mild-to-moderate upper-respiratory infections due to susceptible Group A streptococci (e.g., pharyngitis)
Venereal infections: syphilis, yaws, bejel, and pinta
Prophylaxis of rheumatic fever and/or chorea and recurrent acute glomerulonephritis (follow-up for rheumatic heart disease)

dosage.n: Older pediatric patients: 900,000 units; infants/children under 60 lbs: 300,000-600,000 units

dosage.d: Under 2 years: 50,000 units/kg; ages 2-12 years: adjust based on adult schedule
1,200,000 units once a month OR 600,000 units every 2 weeks

admin: FOR DEEP INTRAMUSCULAR INJECTION ONLY; never give intravenously or admix with IV solutions (risk of cardiorespiratory arrest and death)
Inject in the upper outer quadrant of the buttock (dorsogluteal) or the ventrogluteal site; in neonates/infants/small children prefer the midlateral thigh
Do not inject into or near an artery or nerve; avoid the anterolateral thigh
Inject at a slow, steady rate to avoid needle blockage from suspended material; vary the site on repeat doses
Inspect visually for particulate matter and discoloration before use
moa: Penicillin G exerts a bactericidal action against penicillin-susceptible organisms during active multiplication by inhibiting the biosynthesis of cell-wall peptidoglycan, rendering the cell wall osmotically unstable. The benzathine salt has very low solubility and is slowly hydrolyzed to penicillin G at the IM site, producing low but prolonged serum levels.

absolute: History of a previous hypersensitivity (anaphylactic) reaction to any penicillin
Intravenous or intra-arterial administration (boxed warning - risk of cardiorespiratory arrest and death)
relative: History of significant allergies and/or asthma
monitor: Signs of hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis for an appropriate period after injection
Injection site for neurovascular compromise (pallor, mottling, cyanosis, pain)

preg: Reproduction studies in mouse, rat, and rabbit revealed no evidence of impaired fertility or harm to the fetus, and human experience with penicillins in pregnancy has not shown positive evidence of adverse fetal effects. There are, however, no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women; use during pregnancy only if clearly needed.
lact: Soluble penicillin G (the hydrolysate of penicillin G benzathine) is excreted in breast milk. Caution should be exercised when penicillin G benzathine is administered to a nursing woman.
renal: Penicillin G is substantially excreted by the kidney, and the risk of toxic reactions may be greater in patients with impaired renal function; excretion is considerably delayed in renal impairment and in neonates and young infants. Monitor renal function and select dose cautiously, particularly in the elderly.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dosage adjustment is provided in the labeling.

major: Tetracycline (bacteriostatic) may antagonize the bactericidal effect of penicillin; avoid concurrent use
moderate: Probenecid increases and prolongs serum penicillin levels by inhibiting renal tubular secretion
interactions.diagnostics: May cause elevated BUN, creatinine, and SGOT; can affect culture results.

serious: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SJS, TEN, DRESS, AGEP)
Neurovascular injury from inadvertent intravascular/perineural injection (Nicolau syndrome, gangrene, transverse myelitis with permanent paralysis)
rare: Cardiorespiratory arrest from inadvertent IV administration
emergency: Anaphylaxis (treat immediately with epinephrine, oxygen, airway management)
Cardiorespiratory arrest after inadvertent intravenous injection
Limb ischemia/neurovascular compromise at injection site

monitoring: Observe for hypersensitivity reactions after injection
Inquire about prior penicillin/cephalosporin/allergen reactions before dosing
Monitor injection site for signs of vascular compromise
Watch for C. difficile-associated diarrhea (may occur up to 2 months later)
counsel: Tell your provider about any prior reaction to penicillins, cephalosporins, or other drugs before the injection
This medicine is given as a deep injection into muscle, never into a vein
Report rash, hives, swelling, difficulty breathing, or severe pain at the injection site right away
Contact your provider for watery or bloody diarrhea, even weeks after the injection
Complete the full prescribed course/schedule, especially for strep and prophylaxis
pk: Bactericidal serum levels achieved soon after IM injection
Low peak levels; 300,000 units gives 0.03-0.05 units/mL
Very prolonged: levels persist ~14 days after 1,200,000 units; detectable up to 4 weeks
Store in a refrigerator, 2-8 C (36-46 F); keep from freezing
pearls: NOT for intravenous use - inadvertent IV administration has caused cardiorespiratory arrest and death (boxed warning)
Long-acting depot ideal for one-time strep treatment, single-dose early syphilis, and monthly rheumatic-fever prophylaxis
Penicillin G resistance has not been reported in Streptococcus pyogenes
Inadvertent intra-arterial or perineural injection can cause gangrene and permanent paralysis; inject deep IM, avoiding vessels and nerves
Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction may follow syphilis treatment
missed: For monthly or biweekly prophylaxis, administer a missed dose as soon as possible and resume the regular schedule. Do not skip doses, as inadequate therapy in streptococcal disease may allow sequelae to develop.
overdose: Penicillin in overdosage may cause neuromuscular hyperirritability or convulsive seizures. Management is supportive; control seizures and provide standard supportive care.
